Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 system prompt just leaked.
1500+ lines of the most detailed AI safety rules ever written.
Here's the wildest thing I found:
Claude has opinions. It's just told not to share them.
"Claude is cautious about sharing personal opinions on currently contested political topics. It needn't deny having opinions, but can decline to share them."
It gets weirder.
The prompt explicitly bans self-harm counseling techniques like "hold an ice cube" or "snap a rubber band." Anthropic's reasoning: they mimic the sensation of self-harm and reinforce the pattern.
Instead of interrupting — they make it worse.
But here's the part nobody is talking about:
Claude Fable 5 has a secret twin. Same underlying model. Fewer safety restrictions.
It's called Claude Mythos 5 — an uncensored version available only to "approved organizations."
One model. Two personalities. One locked, one hidden.
The most intelligent AI is also the most tightly controlled.
And the demand for the uncensored version is real enough that Anthropic built one — just not for you.
Full breakdown → https://t.co/wKdJu4oQFE

On Friday the US government switched off the most capable AI on earth.

At 5:21pm Eastern, @AnthropicAI received a letter. Citing national security, the government ordered it to suspend access to its two most advanced models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, for any foreign national anywhere in the world. Cloud software has no borders, so the only way to comply was to shut the models down for everyone, in every country, at once.

The stated reason? A jailbreak that amounted to asking the model to read a codebase and fix its flaws. Developers call that debugging. They do it every day. The government called it a cyber-weapon.

Aesop warned us about the bear who crushed his master's skull to kill a fly. This week the Commerce Department played the bear, and @claudeai Fable 5 was the fly. The fly is dead. Look what happened to the master.

Here is the part that should worry every business building on AI. If Washington can flip the kill switch on a Friday afternoon over a debugging prompt, no enterprise can treat frontier AI as stable infrastructure. You do not build a factory on land the state can repossess without notice.

And it happened on the same Friday @SpaceX floated to make @elonmusk  the world's first paper trillionaire, his wealth now north of 4 per cent of American GDP. One state, one afternoon. It found the will to brick an AI model in hours, and no will at all to ask what it means for one person to own a slice of the world.

We broke up Standard Oil with a court order. We are building Standard Everything with a tax break.

This week's issue of The Sunday Signal is out now. Full essay, the historical pattern that says this never ends quietly, and the weekly layoff tracker.

What would you build your business on, knowing the supplier can be switched off by a third party you never signed a contract with?

That’s exactly what your AI bill looks like when a top-tier model like Fable 5 is being used to do the work of a simple linter. 

Most teams burn through four-figure API bills because of a psychological factor: the fear of getting a bad result. They pick the biggest model at $50 per million output tokens and run refactoring, docstrings, and minor formatting fixes through it. That’s financial suicide.

The key rule of optimization is simple: a model is a gear shifter, not a fixed button.

Instead of relying on a “universal genius,” successful developers redesign their systems around an architecture where a cheap crew is managed by one expensive brain. 

Routine work and boilerplate code generation are handled by Sonnet 4.6 ($15/1M) by default. If a task is genuinely difficult or security-critical, it is automatically escalated to Opus 4.8. Meanwhile, result verification (grading) with simple yes/no decisions is performed by Haiku 4.5, which costs ten times less than the flagship model 

The creator should never grade their own homework, and it certainly makes no sense to pay Fable 5 rates for that job 

This approach completely changes the economics of software development. 

When you separate routine tasks by complexity, enable prompt caching for static context, and send background jobs through the Batch API at half price, your final bill can drop by 71% while maintaining the same code quality [indexes: text].

Start small: move all validation checks and log analysis to Haiku and see what happens to your balance by next week.

@elder_plinius What actually happened
Within ~1 day, prolific jailbreaker Pliny the Liberator publicly posted a multi-agent “pack hunt” bypass using techniques like:
•  Unicode/homoglyph tricks (e.g., Cyrillic substitutions)
•  Long-context framing
•  Fiction/academic wrappers
•  Query decomposition + reassembly
This got the model to output things like stack buffer overflow exploit code, Birch reduction chem synthesis steps, and even leaked Fable’s massive ~120k-character system prompt. @elder_plinius 
Anthropic’s take (from their official statement): This was narrow/non-universal, replicated similar minor/known vuln-finding on other models (including OpenAI’s), produced no harmful real-world uplift, and didn’t defeat the core safeguards broadly. They stand by their approach but acknowledge perfect resistance isn’t here yet. anthropic
The US government (via Commerce, after Amazon researchers flagged/duplicated issues and calls with Dario Amodei) saw it differently—national security risk from exposed cyber capabilities in a dual-use model. They issued an export control directive barring all foreign nationals (even inside the US, including Anthropic’s own staff). Since API keys can’t reliably enforce nationality at scale, Anthropic disabled Fable 5 and Mythos 5 globally for everyone to comply. Other Claude models are unaffected.

Anthropic launched Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on June 9. On June 12, a US export-control order forced them to turn both models off for everyone.

That’s three days from “this is our newest, most powerful release” to “you can’t use this at all,” for reasons no customer controlled.

Practically, it’s an ownership question. Companies don’t get to own frontier models. You rent them. You do get to own your data, your workflows, your review layers, your prompts, your compliance logic, and the way your team thinks about where AI is allowed to touch the work. Those are the pieces that still belong to you when a model disappears for a week, or a month, or forever.

If there’s a useful exercise here, I’d say: map your stack and circle what would break if one specific model vanished tomorrow. Anything inside that circle either needs a fallback, or needs to move closer to things you actually control. The goal isn’t to avoid risk. It’s to make sure the hardest parts of what you do don’t belong to someone else’s API.

I found a repo that tries to rebuild the behavior with Opus 4.8 + Fusion:

- Opus 4.8 answers the task once
- a second Opus 4.8 answers blind in parallel
- a third Opus reads both
- it pulls the consensus
- flags where they split
- catches what both missed
- writes the final answer from the cross-exam

One run can sound confident and still be wrong

2 blind runs plus a judge makes the failure much harder to hide

- put the claimed Fable prompt in CLAUDE.md
- run the same task through Fusion-Fable
- compare it against stock Opus 4.8

data.text:
Research that caused the Commerce Department to impose strict limits on the use of Anthropic’s new AI models wasn’t geared toward offensive purposes, according to a cybersecurity CEO who saw the findings.

Late Friday, the department used national security export controls to bar the company from distributing Fable 5 and Mythos 5.

The directive applies to people outside the U.S. and foreign nationals in the U.S., including Anthropic’s own non-citizen employees. Due to the directive’s scope, Anthropic said it had no choice but to disable the models for all users.

The company said it was told that research on a “jailbreak” of Anthropic’s AI that sought to probe bypassing of safeguards sparked the export controls.

“We disagree that the finding of a narrow potential jailbreak should be cause for recalling a commercial model deployed to hundreds of millions of people,” Anthropic wrote in a blog post. “If this standard was applied across the industry, we believe it would essentially halt all new model deployments for all frontier model providers.”

While the company reaffirmed the government’s ability to block unsafe AI, it argued that should be part of a statutory process that’s transparent fair, and based on technical facts. “This action does not adhere to those principles.”

Katie Moussouris, CEO of cybersecurity firm Luta Security, told the Wall Street Journal that Anthropic showed her a copy of the findings, which were produced by Amazon researchers using prompts to obtain information about security vulnerabilities.

“I’ve seen the paper. It’s not a jailbreak. It was Defense Oriented Prompting (DOP), capabilities defenders need,” she explained in a post on X on Saturday.

Moussouris added, “If Nat defense is the goal, this just scored an own goal against us.”

Amazon and the Commerce Department didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Meanwhile, the administration’s directive barring foreign nationals in the U.S. from using Anthropic’s new models raised alarms.

Ben Murphy, a scholar at the Institute for Progress think tank, called it “another step on the balkanization of technology.”

“It might previously have been unthinkable to require proof-of-citizenship to access services; it’s increasingly common across new technologies and, to be honest, this attempt is not surprising in that light,” he added in a post on X.

Murphy also highlighted the unpredictability of the administration’s actions and its consequence for AI developers, warning that labs could keep more models in-house or not make them available.

In addition, labs might be less inclined toward engaging with the government about potential vulnerabilities, he said, with Anthropic’s stance on being transparent seeming to backfire.

Anthropic was already feuding with the administration, which has deemed it a supply-chain risk for Pentagon contractors. Still, the company provided early access to the Mythos model as it warned on its potential cybersecurity implications.

“I don’t know that the government wouldn’t have reached that conclusion themselves, but as a business matter, those pronouncements have not produced a healthy working relationship with the government,” Murphy wrote.
